practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how Spain built an imperial system in the Caribbean between 1503 and 1518. You may use the following in your answer: the founding of the Casa de Contratacion (1503), the formalising of the encomienda system (1503). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order they happened.

Indicative content:
• The 1503 founding of the Casa de Contratacion in Seville created a single royal agency to license every ship, sailor and cargo crossing the Atlantic — capturing the royal fifth and shutting out non-Castilian rivals.
• In the same year the encomienda system was formalised, ‘entrusting’ Indigenous workers to settlers in exchange for tribute and Christian instruction — this was the labour mechanism the Casa’s wealth depended on.
• The brutality of encomienda on Hispaniola provoked the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos’s 1511 sermon — the first public protest against the treatment of Indigenous peoples and a sign of an internal Spanish debate growing alongside the empire.
• In 1513 the Requerimiento gave Spanish violence a legal veneer — conquistadors could read it aloud, often unintelligibly, before attacking and then claim a ‘just war’.
• The collapse of the Taino workforce on Hispaniola pushed the Crown to license the first shipments of enslaved Africans to the Indies in 1518 — beginning the transatlantic slave trade and completing the four-pillared system (monopoly, encomienda, missionary, Requerimiento) that Spain would carry to Mexico and Peru.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with clear linkage (‘this in turn forced’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (Montesinos, Requerimiento, asiento). Reaches an analytical overall point.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Antonio de Montesinos’s 1511 sermon for Spanish imperial policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Montesinos’s sermon, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• It was the first public Spanish protest against the treatment of Indigenous peoples in the Americas — demolishing the convenient idea that ‘everyone thought it was acceptable’.
• The sermon scandalised the Hispaniola colonists but reached the Crown — pushing Ferdinand to convene the meetings that produced the Laws of Burgos (1512), the first attempt to regulate encomienda.
• It influenced the young encomendero Bartolome de las Casas, who would become the most determined campaigner for Indigenous rights and a central figure in the New Laws of 1542.
• It set the precedent that Catholic mission and imperial extraction were in tension — a tension that would run through the whole period and produce the Las Casas–Sepulveda debate of 1550–51.
• It established that the moral case for Spanish empire could be challenged from within the Spanish Church itself — not from outside, by Protestants, but from inside, by Dominicans.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail (the date 1511, the Laws of Burgos 1512, the influence on Las Casas).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the sermon without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Requerimiento (from 1513) for Spanish conduct in the Americas.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the Requerimiento, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Requerimiento gave Spanish violence a legal veneer — if Indigenous peoples did not accept the Pope and the Spanish king, war could be declared a ‘just war’ under Spanish law.
• It allowed conquistadors to argue that captives from war were lawful enslaved spoils, not protected royal subjects — with direct consequences for the slave trade in Indigenous prisoners.
• It was often read in Spanish or Latin at dawn, sometimes from offshore — making the legal ‘requirement’ impossible to fulfil and exposing the document as a fig leaf.
• It shaped the conduct of Cortes’s and Pizarro’s expeditions a few years later — both leaders went through the formal motion of reading it before attacking, even when the audience could not understand a word.
• It became a target for critics like Las Casas, who said he did not know whether to laugh at it or weep — using the Requerimiento itself as evidence that Spanish empire needed reform.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail (the 1513 drafting, the legal ‘just war’ doctrine, the link forward to Cortes/Pizarro and Las Casas’s critique).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Requerimiento without explaining its importance.

lessons.title: The Conquistadors Begin: Balboa, Cuba and Magellan
lessons.description: Balboa reaches the Pacific, Cuba is taken, and Magellan’s ship circles the globe.
lessons.content_html:
From Caribbean Foothold to Continental Push

By 1510 Spain had built a colony on Hispaniola but had not yet pushed onto the mainland. Within a decade that changed completely. In 1513 Vasco Nunez de Balboa walked across the isthmus of Panama and saw the Pacific Ocean. Between 1511 and 1515, Diego Velazquez conquered Cuba and made it the staging post for everything that came next. In 1519–22 Ferdinand Magellan’s expedition sailed across the Pacific and the surviving ship circled the globe. By 1520 Spain had a Caribbean base, a Pacific shore, and a transpacific reach — the platform Cortes and Pizarro would use for the great mainland conquests of Mexico and Peru. This lesson follows the three steps that made the launch pad.

Balboa Reaches the Pacific (1513)

Vasco Nunez de Balboa was the unlikeliest founder of a Pacific empire. A failed pig farmer on Hispaniola, in debt, he stowed away in a barrel on a 1510 expedition to the Caribbean coast of South America. By the time the barrel was discovered at sea, the expedition had no choice but to take him on. Within a year he had become governor of Spain’s small foothold at Darien, in present-day Panama, by ousting his rival in a coup. From local Indigenous informants Balboa heard that, just over the mountains to the south, lay another sea and a kingdom rich in gold — what we now call Peru.

On 1 September 1513, Balboa set out with around 190 Spaniards, several hundred Indigenous porters and a pack of war dogs. They cut their way through 65 miles of mountainous tropical forest. On 25 September 1513, alone on a peak, Balboa saw a glittering ocean to the south. He came down to the shore, waded into the surf in full armour, and claimed the entire ocean — which he called the South Sea — for the Spanish Crown. He was the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas.

Key Fact

On 25 September 1513, Vasco Nunez de Balboa became the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas. He waded into the surf in armour and claimed the ‘South Sea’ for Spain — opening the door to a westward push that would reach Mexico, Peru and the Philippines.

Balboa’s discovery transformed Spanish strategy. The Pacific was no longer a rumour; it was a Spanish ocean. Crucially, the rumours of a southern empire of gold became official intelligence at the Spanish court — planting the seed of what Pizarro would harvest in 1532. Yet Balboa himself had a short reward: in 1519 his rival Pedrarias Davila, sent as the new royal governor, had him beheaded on a trumped-up charge of treason. The man who claimed the Pacific did not live to use it.

The Conquest of Cuba (1511–15)

While Balboa was crossing the isthmus, another conquistador was conquering an island. In 1511 Diego Velazquez landed on Cuba with around 300 Spaniards and a force of Tainos from Hispaniola. The campaign that followed lasted three years and was brutal. Cuban Tainos resisted under a remarkable cacique called Hatuey, who had fled the slaughter on Hispaniola to warn Cuban communities of what was coming. He told them that the Spanish god was gold, and that if they did not hide it the Spanish would destroy them.

In 1512 Hatuey was captured and burned at the stake. As the flames were lit, a Franciscan friar offered him conversion to Christianity, promising that he would go to heaven. The friar Bartolome de las Casas later recorded Hatuey’s reply: he asked whether Spaniards went to heaven, and when told they did, said he would not go there — for he wanted nothing to do with such cruel people. Hatuey’s martyrdom became one of the most powerful indictments of the conquest in Las Casas’s writings.

Velazquez completed the conquest by 1515 and founded Spanish towns including Santiago de Cuba and Havana. The encomienda system was carried over from Hispaniola, and the Cuban Taino population collapsed under it within a generation. But for Spanish purposes Cuba was now what Hispaniola had been: a base. From the harbours of Santiago and Havana, the next wave of conquistadors — including a young Hernan Cortes — would launch into the mainland. Without Cuba, there is no Mexico in 1519.

Students often write about ‘the Spanish’ as one block. The reality is messier. Velazquez, having conquered Cuba, became its governor and tried to control who launched expeditions from it. He fell out with Cortes in 1519 and tried to recall him from Mexico. Pedrarias Davila, the new governor of Panama, had Balboa beheaded as a political rival in 1519. The conquistadors competed bitterly with each other for governorships, encomiendas, royal favour and the right to launch the next expedition. Showing this internal Spanish conflict is a top-band move — the empire was not a single project but a tournament between conquistadors that the Crown supervised and (eventually) controlled.

Magellan’s Voyage (1519–22)

The third leg of the conquistador platform was not a conquest but a voyage. Ferdinand Magellan was a Portuguese navigator who, after falling out with the Portuguese Crown, offered his services to the young King Charles I of Spain (later Holy Roman Emperor Charles V). Charles wanted a westward route to the Spice Islands of the East Indies — the source of the cloves, nutmeg and pepper that fed Europe’s appetite for spices — that did not infringe Portugal’s eastward route around Africa under the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494).

Magellan sailed from Seville on 10 August 1519 with five ships and around 270 men. After mutinies, ice storms in the south Atlantic and the discovery of the strait that still bears his name at the southern tip of South America, he crossed the Pacific in 99 brutal weeks — some crewmen ate leather and rats — and reached the islands he named for Saint Lazarus, today the Philippines. There, in April 1521, he was killed in a skirmish at the Battle of Mactan after intervening in a local power struggle.

The expedition continued under his Basque second-in-command, Juan Sebastian Elcano. Of the five original ships and around 270 men, only one ship, the Victoria, and 18 men returned to Seville on 6 September 1522. They had become the first humans known to have circled the globe.

Key Fact

Magellan’s expedition (1519–22) gave Spain its claim to the Philippines and produced the first circumnavigation of the globe. Magellan was killed in the Philippines in April 1521; Juan Sebastian Elcano brought the Victoria home in September 1522 with only 18 of the original 270 men.

Why It Mattered

The Spanish claim to the Philippines, founded on Magellan’s voyage, would last until 1898 and gave Spain a foothold in Asia that pulled silk, porcelain and spices through Mexican ports across the Pacific. The Pacific was now visibly a Spanish ocean — reached by Balboa from the east, crossed by Magellan from the west. Combined with Cuba as a Caribbean staging post, Spain had the geography it needed for the next, biggest moves: Cortes’s expedition to Mexico in 1519 (launched from Santiago de Cuba while Velazquez tried in vain to recall him), and Pizarro’s push into Peru in 1532 (built on the rumours Balboa had collected on the Pacific shore).

Examiners flag the trap of writing three mini-paragraphs as if Balboa, Cuba and Magellan were unrelated. They are not. Balboa’s 1513 Pacific opened the strategic question that Magellan’s 1519–22 voyage answered: how do we cross it? The Cuban conquest of 1511–15 supplied the men, ships and food that Cortes used in 1519 to launch westward into Mexico, completing the platform. Top-band analytical narratives chain these stages with phrases like ‘this in turn made possible’ or ‘because of this’ rather than treating them as separate events.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark Analytical Narrative questions on the early conquistadors, examiners specifically flag answers that read like a chronological list (‘first Balboa did X, then Velazquez did Y, then Magellan did Z’). The top-band move is to chain stages with explicit linkage — Balboa’s Pacific opens the strategic question, the Cuban conquest builds the launch pad, Magellan’s voyage proves a Pacific crossing is possible. For Explain the Importance questions, anchor the importance in named consequences (Cortes launches from Santiago, Pizarro acts on Balboa’s intelligence) rather than vague claims like ‘it was very important’. Use precise vocabulary — cacique, isthmus, Spice Islands, encomienda — for SPaG marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • On 25 September 1513, Vasco Nunez de Balboa became the first European to reach the Pacific from the Americas, claiming the ‘South Sea’ for Spain and gathering the rumours of a southern empire of gold that would lead to Peru.
  • Diego Velazquez conquered Cuba (1511–15), founding Santiago and Havana — the Indigenous resistance leader Hatuey was burned at the stake in 1512 — and turning the island into the staging post from which Cortes would launch his Mexican expedition.
  • Magellan’s expedition (1519–22) gave Spain a Pacific crossing and a claim to the Philippines; Magellan was killed in 1521 and Elcano brought the Victoria home in 1522 to complete the first circumnavigation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Balboa’s 1513 expedition for the later Spanish empire in the Americas.

Indicative content:

• His claim of the ‘South Sea’ for Spain opened the door to a westward push that would reach Mexico, Peru and the Philippines, anchoring the long-term shape of the empire.
• The Indigenous intelligence Balboa gathered about a southern empire of gold became official Spanish knowledge at court — planting the seed Pizarro acted on in 1532 when he sailed for Peru.
• The new Spanish foothold in Panama, including Panama City founded in 1519, became the bridgehead from which Pizarro’s expedition was launched.
• Balboa’s 1519 execution by Pedrarias Davila showed how political the conquistador era was — a forerunner of the rivalries between Cortes and Velazquez and Pizarro and Almagro.

• The first circumnavigation under Elcano in 1522 demonstrated that the Pacific could be crossed, integrating the new Spanish empire into a single global commercial system.
• The voyage created the geographic conditions for the later Manila Galleon, which carried American silver to Asia and Asian silk and porcelain back through Mexican ports.
• The huge cost — only one ship and 18 of around 270 men returned — underlined how dangerous Pacific crossings were and shaped how Spain regulated transatlantic and trans-Pacific shipping.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on Magellan’s voyage without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how Spain built a launching pad for the conquest of the mainland between 1511 and 1522. You may use the following in your answer: Balboa reaching the Pacific (1513), the conquest of Cuba (1511–15). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order they happened.

Indicative content:
• Diego Velazquez conquered Cuba between 1511 and 1515, founding Santiago and Havana — ports that turned the island into a staging post for further expeditions, and a place to recruit men, breed horses and build ships.
• While the Cuban conquest was underway, Balboa crossed the isthmus of Panama in September 1513 and saw the Pacific — opening a strategic question (how to cross it?) and gathering Indigenous intelligence about a southern empire of gold.
• This in turn drove Spanish thinking westward: rumours of a Pacific empire of gold became official intelligence at court, planting the seed for Pizarro’s Peruvian expedition in 1532.
• In 1519–22 Magellan’s expedition (under Elcano after Magellan’s death) crossed the Pacific and answered the strategic question Balboa had opened — proving the Pacific could be sailed and giving Spain a claim to the Philippines.
• Because of all this, when Hernan Cortes left Santiago de Cuba in February 1519, he was launching from the platform Cuba had built, on the Pacific-facing strategic frontier Balboa had opened — and into a continent that Magellan’s voyage was about to turn into part of a global Spanish commercial system.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with clear linkage (‘this in turn made possible’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (Magellan, Pedrarias Davila, the link forward to Cortes and Pizarro). Reaches an analytical overall point.
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Cuba as a Spanish base in the period 1515–19.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Cuba, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Cuba supplied the men, horses, ships and provisions that supported every Spanish expedition into the western Caribbean and onto the mainland in this period.
• Santiago de Cuba was the port from which Hernan Cortes launched his expedition to Mexico in February 1519 — without Cuba, there is no Mexico in 1519.
• As governor of Cuba, Diego Velazquez tried to control which expeditions left from his island and to recall those that defied him — making Cuba a stage for conquistador rivalry as well as conquest.
• Cuban Taino communities, devastated by encomienda and disease within a generation, were the workforce that fed and supported the Spanish forces preparing for mainland war.
• The conquest of Cuba also produced figures like the friar Bartolome de las Casas, who began as a young encomendero on the island and would later become the most determined Spanish critic of conquest.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail (Velazquez, Cortes’s 1519 expedition, the Taino population collapse).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Cuba without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Spanish claim to the Philippines after Magellan’s voyage.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the Spanish claim to the Philippines, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Spanish claim, founded on Magellan’s voyage of 1519–22, gave Spain a permanent foothold in Asia that lasted until 1898 — the only major European Asian colony reached from the Americas.
• The Philippines became the western terminus of the later Manila Galleon trade, which carried American silver to Asia and Asian silk and porcelain back through Mexican ports.
• Combined with Balboa’s 1513 Pacific claim, the Philippines turned the Pacific into a Spanish ocean and made the empire genuinely global.
• The voyage demonstrated that Tordesillas-compliant westward routes existed — Spain could reach the spice trade without infringing Portugal’s African and Indian Ocean monopoly.
• It made the Spanish silver economy of the Andes (after 1545) part of a single Pacific commercial system — the world’s first global currency was Spanish silver shipped through Manila.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands, with specific period detail (the 1521 landing, the link to Tordesillas, the connection to silver and the Manila Galleon).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the Philippines claim without explaining its importance.

lessons.title: Cortes and the Conquest of Mexico
lessons.description: Cortes’s 1519 expedition, the Tlaxcalan alliance, smallpox, and the fall of Tenochtitlan.
lessons.content_html:
Leaving Cuba, February 1519

In February 1519, Hernan Cortes sailed from Santiago de Cuba with around 500 men, 16 horses and 14 cannon. Diego Velazquez, the governor of Cuba, had originally commissioned the expedition but tried to recall it at the last minute, suspecting Cortes would not stay loyal once he had reached the mainland. Velazquez was right. From the moment Cortes landed at Vera Cruz on the Mexican coast in April 1519, he was operating outside Velazquez’s authority — technically, in defiance of his governor. To make sure his men could not change their minds, Cortes scuttled most of his ships at Vera Cruz, deliberately stranding the expedition on the mainland. (He did not, despite the legend, burn them.)

Key Fact

Cortes left Santiago de Cuba in February 1519 with around 500 men, 16 horses and 14 cannon, defying his governor Velazquez. He scuttled (not burned) his ships at Vera Cruz to commit his men to the inland march.

The Aztec Empire in 1519

The state Cortes was about to challenge was not a fragile kingdom. The Aztec or Mexica Empire of central Mexico ruled from the lake city of Tenochtitlan (population 200,000+, larger than any city in Spain) and extracted tribute from millions of subjects across modern-day Mexico. Its emperor was Montezuma II, a senior priest-king. Its religion required regular human sacrifice. But its empire had been built by force, not consent: the tribute peoples around its edges, including the independent state of Tlaxcala, had grown to hate Aztec rule. Cortes did not bring down the Aztec Empire on his own; he weaponised the resentment its subjects already felt.

The Tlaxcalan Alliance

After landing, Cortes marched inland with his small Spanish force and a translator he had been given as a slave: La Malinche (also called Dona Marina). She spoke both Nahuatl and a Mayan language; combined with Geronimo de Aguilar, a Spaniard who spoke Mayan after years of captivity, she gave Cortes a route into Aztec politics. The Tlaxcalans, who were not subjects of the Aztecs and resented their tribute demands, fought a brief war with Cortes in September 1519 — and then accepted alliance with him. Tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan warriors would fight on the Spanish side for the next two years.

No. The historian Matthew Restall’s ‘Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest’ calls this the central myth of the period. The conquest was not a few hundred Spaniards crushing the Aztec Empire. It was a coalition war, with the Tlaxcalans — tens of thousands of Indigenous warriors — doing the bulk of the fighting alongside a Spanish core. Spanish steel, horses, gunpowder and crossbows mattered, but they did not decide the war on their own. Smallpox, Aztec internal divisions, the resentment of tribute peoples and Cortes’s political skill all mattered more. Top-band judgement answers reject the ‘Cortes the genius’ framing and weigh these factors against each other.

Cortes Meets Montezuma

In November 1519, Cortes was welcomed into Tenochtitlan by Montezuma II. The Spanish were given a palace to stay in and treated as honoured guests — though they were also, effectively, surrounded. Within weeks, Cortes seized Montezuma in his own palace and held him as a hostage, ruling the empire through him. Whether Montezuma genuinely believed Cortes was the returning god Quetzalcoatl is a Spanish-source claim that modern historians like Camilla Townsend doubt — the prophecy story may have been invented after the conquest by Mexica nobles trying to explain a defeat. What is certain is that Spanish behaviour, including a massacre at the temple festival of Toxcatl in May 1520 led by Cortes’s deputy Pedro de Alvarado, ended any chance that the occupation could remain peaceful.

La Noche Triste, 30 June 1520

A full Aztec uprising broke out. On the night of 30 June 1520 — remembered by the Spanish as La Noche Triste, ‘the Sad Night’ — the Spanish tried to escape Tenochtitlan along its causeways under cover of darkness. They were attacked from all sides. Montezuma was killed (whether by Spanish guards or Aztec stones is disputed), and Cortes lost more than half his force, much of his treasure and most of his cannon. The Spanish stumbled out into Tlaxcalan territory, broken but alive. They had been driven from Tenochtitlan in catastrophe.

Smallpox in Tenochtitlan, Autumn 1520

In the autumn of 1520, smallpox arrived in Tenochtitlan with a captured Spanish soldier — and devastated the city. Cuitlahuac, the new emperor who had led the resistance on the Noche Triste, died of the disease after only 80 days on the throne. The Aztec leadership, military command, priests and ordinary people died together; survivors had to walk over bodies in the streets. By the time Cortes returned to besiege the city in 1521, the empire he was attacking had already lost a substantial portion of its population and most of its experienced commanders. Disease — not skill at arms — bought the Spanish coalition the time it needed to regroup.

Key Fact

Smallpox struck Tenochtitlan in autumn 1520 and killed the new Aztec emperor Cuitlahuac after just 80 days on the throne. The epidemic destroyed Aztec leadership and weakened the city before the final siege began.

The Siege of Tenochtitlan, 1521

Cortes spent the winter rebuilding. In Tlaxcala, Spanish carpenters and Tlaxcalan workers built thirteen brigantines — small armed sailing ships — in pieces, then carried them in sections over the mountains to Lake Texcoco and assembled them. Tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan warriors joined a Spanish core of around 700 men. From May 1521 the brigantines blockaded Tenochtitlan’s causeways while the coalition cut off the city’s aqueducts, food and water. The last Aztec emperor, Cuauhtemoc, organised a fierce defence street by street.

The city fell on 13 August 1521. An estimated 100,000 Aztec defenders and civilians died in the siege; Tenochtitlan itself was systematically demolished and the new colonial capital, Mexico City, was built on its ruins. Cuauhtemoc was captured trying to escape across the lake. He was kept alive for several years before being executed by Cortes in 1525 on a march through Honduras — a quiet, lawless killing that sealed the political end of the Mexica imperial line.

Examiners reward students who weigh several factors against each other rather than collapsing the conquest into one cause. The Tlaxcalan alliance provided most of the warriors and local intelligence. Smallpox killed the Aztec leadership at the worst possible moment. The empire’s tribute system had alienated subject peoples, who defected to Cortes’s coalition. Spanish steel, horses, crossbows and brigantines mattered — especially on the lake — but were not decisive on their own. La Malinche’s linguistic and political skill made the alliance possible. Cortes’s leadership was real but cannot stand alone. The Restall view is that this was a coalition victory over a fractured empire, not a Spanish miracle.

After the Fall

Cortes was made first Governor and Captain-General of New Spain in 1523, but the Crown distrusted independent conquistadors. By 1528 he had been recalled to Spain, given titles and estates but stripped of the governorship; the bureaucracy of the Casa de Contratacion, audiencia and (from 1535) viceroyalty took over. The lesson Madrid learned from Cortes was the same one it had learned from Columbus: conquistadors were too dangerous to leave in charge of conquered territory.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 16-mark Make and Defend a Judgement questions on the conquest of Mexico, the trap is collapsing the win into one factor — usually ‘Cortes’s leadership’ or ‘Spanish weapons’. Top-band answers weigh several factors (Tlaxcalan numbers, smallpox in 1520, Aztec internal divisions, Spanish steel and horses, Cortes’s leadership) against each other and reach a substantiated overall judgement. For Analytical Narrative questions, chain events with phrases like ‘this in turn forced’ rather than describing them sequentially. Use precise vocabulary — Mexica, Tlaxcalan, La Noche Triste, brigantine, cacique, encomienda — for SPaG marks, and write ‘Indigenous peoples’ rather than older terms.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cortes left Santiago de Cuba in February 1519 with around 500 men in defiance of Velazquez, scuttled his ships at Vera Cruz, and built a Tlaxcalan alliance whose tens of thousands of warriors made the conquest possible.
  • After meeting Montezuma in November 1519 and seizing him as a hostage, the Spanish were driven out on La Noche Triste (30 June 1520) — but smallpox in autumn 1520 killed the new emperor Cuitlahuac and gutted the Aztec leadership before Cortes returned.
  • Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521 after a brutal siege; the last emperor Cuauhtemoc was captured. The conquest was a coalition victory shaped by Tlaxcalan numbers, smallpox and Aztec divisions — not a solo Spanish miracle.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Tlaxcalan alliance for the Spanish conquest of Mexico.
practice_questions.marks:

Indicative content:
• The Tlaxcalans, an independent Nahua state who had resisted Aztec domination for generations, supplied tens of thousands of warriors who did the bulk of the fighting in the campaigns of 1519–21.
• They gave Cortes local intelligence on Aztec politics, geography and tribute structures — intelligence the small Spanish force could not have gathered for itself.
• Tlaxcalan territory provided refuge after La Noche Triste in June 1520 and the workforce that helped build the thirteen brigantines used in the siege of Tenochtitlan.
• The alliance reframes the conquest as a coalition victory rather than a Spanish solo achievement — which is exactly the analytical move historians like Matthew Restall reward.
• The Tlaxcalans negotiated favourable terms after the conquest — their city kept its autonomy under New Spain — demonstrating that they were genuine allies, not subjects.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the fall of Tenochtitlan on 13 August 1521 for the Spanish empire in the Americas.
practice_questions.marks:

lessons.title: Cortes as Governor and the Spanish Base at Panama
lessons.description: Cortes’s rule over New Spain, the consequences for the Aztecs, and the Pacific base at Panama.
lessons.content_html:
From Conqueror to Governor

Tenochtitlan had fallen on 13 August 1521. Two years later, in October 1523, Emperor Charles V appointed Hernan Cortes as Captain-General and Governor of New Spain. The appointment confirmed Cortes’s victory at the expense of his old rival Diego Velazquez, the governor of Cuba who had originally tried to recall the expedition. For the next five years, Cortes governed an enormous, half-conquered territory at almost ten thousand kilometres from Madrid — a distance that gave him real local power, but that also made the crown deeply nervous.

Key Fact

Cortes ruled New Spain as Governor and Captain-General from 1523 to 1528. Charles V then recalled him to Spain and replaced his personal rule with the audiencia — a royal court of judges directly answerable to Madrid.

Rebuilding Mexico City

Cortes’s first project as governor was to rebuild the ruined Aztec capital. The siege of 1521 had levelled Tenochtitlan; surviving Indigenous labourers were now forced to clear the rubble of their own city and build a Spanish capital on top. Mexico City rose on the same lake island grid — the cathedral was placed on the site of the Templo Mayor, the viceregal palace on the ruins of Montezuma’s palace, and the Plaza Mayor over the old Aztec ceremonial square. The geography of central Mexico City today is the geography of Tenochtitlan with Spanish stone laid over Mexica foundations.

Encomiendas and the New Aristocracy

Cortes also rewarded his men. He granted encomiendas — rights to Indigenous tribute and labour — to his Spanish soldiers, in many cases recycling the Aztec tribute lists wholesale. The maize, cotton and labour that had once flowed to Tenochtitlan now flowed to Spanish encomenderos instead. Crucially, the people doing the carrying did not change. The encomienda was not a new economy; it was the old Aztec tribute economy with new owners on top. Franciscan and Dominican friars arrived from 1524 onwards to convert the Indigenous population — the Twelve Apostles of Mexico, Franciscans who landed in May 1524, are the most famous group — and missions began alongside the encomiendas.

Mostly, no — not at first. The encomienda inherited the Aztec tribute system. The same Nahua communities that had paid maize, cotton and labour to Tenochtitlan now paid them to Spanish encomenderos. What changed was the destination of the tribute and the layer of Catholic worship laid on top. New economic structures — silver mining, the trans-Pacific Manila trade, the sugar economy — would come later. Top-band answers note this continuity: in the short term, the conquest changed who was at the top, not how the bottom worked.

Why Cortes Was Recalled

By 1526 Cortes had marched south on a long, costly expedition to Honduras (1524–26) hunting down a rebellious lieutenant; the journey took him out of the capital for almost two years and his enemies used the absence well. Rivals at the Spanish court accused him of corruption, of withholding the king’s share of treasure, of executing the captured Aztec emperor Cuauhtemoc on the Honduras march in 1525, and — most damaging of all — of behaving like an independent prince. Charles V had a simple rule: a conquistador who built a kingdom of his own was a problem. In 1528 Cortes was recalled to Spain. He was given titles and estates (the marquisate of the Valley of Oaxaca) but stripped of the governorship. Royal power in New Spain was handed to the first audiencia in 1528, and from 1535 to a Viceroy.

Key Fact

Cortes was recalled in 1528 because the crown distrusted any conquistador who became too powerful and independent. He was replaced first by the audiencia (royal court) in 1528 and then by the Viceroy of New Spain in 1535.

Consequences for the Aztecs

For the Mexica and the wider Nahua world, the consequences of conquest unfolded on several timescales. The immediate consequences were the most visible: the demolition of Tenochtitlan, the execution of priests and rulers, the burning of codices, the systematic dismantling of the temple priesthood. The medium-term consequences were demographic. Central Mexico’s population is estimated to have fallen from somewhere between 15 and 25 million people in 1519 to perhaps 1 to 2 million by 1600 — the deadliest collapse in recorded human history. Smallpox in 1520, measles in 1531, typhus in 1545 and again in 1576: each wave killed a generation of people who had no immunity, while forced labour, malnutrition and the loss of land made survivors easier to kill the next time.

But the long-term picture also shows survival. The Nahuatl language continued to be spoken by millions and was written down in alphabetic script by Indigenous scribes (often working with Franciscans). Nahua codex-painting traditions adapted to Catholic subjects rather than disappearing. Local cabildos — town councils — preserved a layer of Indigenous self-government under the Spanish empire. Catholic worship absorbed Indigenous symbolism: the cult of the Virgin of Guadalupe (from 1531) drew on the older shrine of Tonantzin at the same hilltop. The conquest was catastrophic, but it did not erase Indigenous Mexico.

Panama: A Pacific Gateway

While Cortes was reorganising New Spain, a second front was opening on the Pacific. In 1513 Vasco Nunez de Balboa had crossed the isthmus and become the first European to see the Pacific Ocean from the Americas. The settlement at Darien was rough and unhealthy, but the strategic prize was huge: a base from which Spanish ships could push south down the Pacific coast of South America. In 1519 Pedrarias Davila — the same governor who had Balboa beheaded that year — founded Panama City on the Pacific side of the isthmus. Goods and treasure crossed the narrow neck of land overland by mule train; ships unloaded on one ocean and reloaded on the other.

The significance of Panama was that it gave Spain a continental Pacific port two thousand kilometres south of Mexico. From Panama, Francisco Pizarro, Diego de Almagro and the priest Hernando de Luque organised the expeditions of 1524, 1526 and finally 1530–32 that would bring down the Inca empire. Without Panama, the conquest of Peru — and the silver economy that would underwrite Spanish power for the rest of the century — could not have happened on the timetable that it did.

By 1528 Spain had two platforms in the Americas. New Spain in the north gave it a continental capital, an Indigenous tribute base and an experienced settler population. Panama in the south gave it a Pacific port within sailing range of an Andean empire still unknown to Europeans. The conquest of the Inca, which begins in 1532, is the direct continuation of this lesson — Pizarro launches from Panama, copies Cortes’s coalition-and-capital playbook, and arrives in Peru just as smallpox and a civil war have already broken Inca leadership. The two halves of mainland Spanish America fit together.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 4-mark Consequence questions on this lesson, the trap is staying in the immediate aftermath of the conquest — the burning of codices, the rebuilding of Mexico City — and missing the long-term arc. Top-band answers track consequences for the Aztecs across all three timescales: immediate (massacres, demolition), medium-term (encomienda, demographic collapse from smallpox, measles and typhus) and long-term (Nahuatl survival, hybrid Catholic worship, the Indigenous town councils). For 8-mark Explain the Importance questions on Panama, weigh several strands — the strategic Pacific access, the launching point for Pizarro’s 1530–32 expedition, and the long-term role of the isthmus in Spanish trade. Use precise vocabulary — encomienda, audiencia, Captain-General, codex, Mexica — for SPaG marks, and write ‘Indigenous peoples’ rather than older terms.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cortes was appointed Governor and Captain-General of New Spain in 1523, rebuilt Mexico City on the ruins of Tenochtitlan and granted encomiendas to his men. He was recalled in 1528 because Charles V distrusted independent conquistadors and replaced him first with the audiencia and from 1535 with a Viceroy.
  • The consequences for the Aztecs ran across three timescales: immediate destruction of the temple state, medium-term demographic collapse from smallpox, measles and typhus (population falling from 15–25 million in 1519 to 1–2 million by 1600), and long-term survival of Nahuatl language, codex-painting and Indigenous local government under Spanish rule.
  • Panama City — founded by Pedrarias Davila in 1519 — gave Spain a Pacific gateway. From it, Pizarro launched the expedition that would bring down the Inca empire from 1532, making Panama the strategic link between the two halves of Spanish America.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the foundation of Panama City (1519) for the development of Spanish power in the Americas.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Panama City, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Panama City, founded in 1519 by Pedrarias Davila on the Pacific side of the isthmus, gave Spain a continental Pacific port for the first time — converting Balboa’s 1513 sighting of the Pacific into a permanent base.
• It provided the staging point for the expeditions of Pizarro, Almagro and Luque from 1524 onwards, leading directly to the 1530–32 voyage that would bring down the Inca empire.
• It allowed Spanish goods and treasure to cross the narrow isthmus by mule train, linking the Caribbean and Pacific economies and opening South America to Spanish trade and conquest.
• It illustrates the pattern of Spanish empire-building — a chain of coastal bases (Santo Domingo, Havana, Vera Cruz, Panama) from which the next conquest could be launched.
• Without Panama, the conquest of Peru and the silver economy of the second half of the 16th century could not have developed on the same timetable.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands (e.g. strategic Pacific access AND launchpad for Peru) with specific period detail (Balboa 1513, Pedrarias Davila 1519, Pizarro’s expeditions, the mule trains).

Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of Panama City without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the encomienda system in Cortes’s New Spain (1523–28).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the encomienda, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The encomienda gave Cortes a way to reward his soldiers without needing money — instead of cash, he granted them rights to the labour and tribute of named Indigenous communities, creating an instant settler aristocracy.
• It repurposed the existing Aztec tribute system: the same maize, cotton and labour that had flowed to Tenochtitlan now flowed to Spanish encomenderos. This continuity made the colony economically functional from day one.
• It tied the Christianisation programme to the labour system — encomenderos were nominally responsible for the religious instruction of their workers, which gave the Franciscans and Dominicans access from 1524.
• It became the central political problem of the Spanish empire. The encomenderos became hereditary, powerful and independent, prompting the New Laws of 1542 (the next big intervention by Charles V).
• It set the template for Peru, where the same encomienda model was applied after Pizarro’s conquest.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of importance across at least two strands with specific period detail (the recycling of Aztec tribute, the link forward to the New Laws, the missions).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the encomienda without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Cortes’s recall to Spain in 1528.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Cortes’s recall, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The recall established a key principle of Spanish imperial government: no conquistador, however successful, could be allowed to govern conquered territory indefinitely. The crown distrusted independent power.
• It led directly to the creation of the first audiencia of New Spain in 1528 — a royal court of judges answerable to Madrid — and from 1535 the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Bureaucratic, salaried royal officials replaced personal conquistador rule.
• It signalled to other conquistadors (notably Pizarro in Peru) that Madrid would not tolerate a kingdom-within-a-kingdom — a warning that would matter again at the 1546 conquistador rebellion against the New Laws.
• It softened, but did not erase, the personal power of Cortes — he was given the marquisate of the Valley of Oaxaca and substantial estates, but stripped of executive command.
• It illustrates Charles V’s broader policy of centralising royal authority over the Americas — the same logic that produced the Council of the Indies (1524) and the New Laws (1542).

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (audiencia 1528, viceroyalty 1535, marquisate of Oaxaca, link forward to Pizarro).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the recall without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how Spanish power was extended in the Americas in the years 1519–28. You may use the following in your answer: the foundation of Panama City (1519), the rebuilding of Mexico City (1521–22). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order in which they happened.

Indicative content:
• In 1519 Pedrarias Davila founded Panama City on the Pacific side of the isthmus, giving Spain a base from which expeditions could push south down the Pacific coast — the strategic platform that would later launch Pizarro.
• Meanwhile, Cortes’s coalition with the Tlaxcalans and the smallpox epidemic of 1520 made possible the fall of Tenochtitlan on 13 August 1521 — collapsing the largest Indigenous state Europeans had encountered.
• This in turn allowed the rebuilding of Mexico City on the ruins of Tenochtitlan in 1521–22, with the cathedral built on the Templo Mayor — a continental Spanish capital with a tribute base inherited from the Mexica.
• Because of the new colony’s scale, in 1523 Charles V appointed Cortes Governor and Captain-General of New Spain, and Cortes granted encomiendas to his soldiers and welcomed the Franciscan missions of 1524.
• This in turn created the political problem that defined the rest of the period: the conquistadors had become powerful enough to alarm Madrid. By 1528 Cortes had been recalled and the audiencia installed. Spanish power was no longer in conquistador hands — it was being centralised under the crown.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with explicit linkage (‘this in turn forced’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (Tlaxcalans, smallpox, encomienda, audiencia).
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

lessons.title: Pizarro and the Conquest of the Incas
lessons.description: How Pizarro exploited an Inca civil war to capture Atahualpa at Cajamarca, and why Cuzco fell.
lessons.content_html:
Reconnaissance, 1528

Spanish ships had been pushing south down the Pacific coast of South America from Panama since the early 1520s. The expedition that mattered was the third one. In 1528 Francisco Pizarro — an illegitimate, illiterate veteran from Trujillo in Spain who had been with Balboa when the Pacific was first reached — landed briefly on the Inca coast at Tumbes. He saw a wealthy, organised society he had not expected. He saw enough cloth, gold and well-built towns to know there was a major civilisation to the south. He returned to Spain in 1529 and, in the Capitulation of Toledo (signed by Queen Isabella of Portugal as regent in July 1529), secured the legal and royal authority to lead a full conquest expedition.

The Death of Huayna Capac

While Pizarro was lobbying in Spain, the Inca empire was destroying itself. Around 1527, the Inca emperor Huayna Capac died suddenly in the northern city of Quito, alongside his named heir. Spanish chroniclers and modern epidemiologists agree the most likely cause was smallpox — the disease that had reached Tenochtitlan in 1520 had moved south through Indigenous trade routes faster than the Spaniards themselves, and arrived in the Andes years before the conquistadors did. The empire suddenly had no recognised emperor. Two of Huayna Capac’s sons claimed the throne instead: Huascar, the legitimate heir based in the southern capital Cuzco, and Atahualpa, his half-brother in the north, who had the loyalty of the empire’s veteran armies.

Key Fact

Huayna Capac’s death (c.1527, probably from smallpox arriving ahead of the Spaniards) split the Inca empire between Huascar in Cuzco (legitimate) and Atahualpa in Quito (military). Atahualpa won the civil war just weeks before Pizarro arrived.

The Inca Civil War, 1529–32

Atahualpa’s veteran northern army marched south against Cuzco. The campaign culminated in spring 1532 with Atahualpa’s general Quizquiz capturing Huascar at the battle of Quipaipan. Indigenous chronicles describe massacres of Huascar’s family and supporters — the empire was, in effect, two warring states. Atahualpa was on his way south to be crowned in Cuzco when news reached him that strange bearded men had landed on the coast.

Pizarro’s 1530–32 Expedition

Pizarro sailed from Panama in January 1531 with about 168 men, 62 horses and a handful of cannon. He brought his half-brothers Hernando, Juan and Gonzalo Pizarro, his partner Diego de Almagro, the Dominican friar Vicente de Valverde and the Indigenous interpreter Felipillo. They landed at the Bay of San Mateo and marched down the coast through the early months of 1532, founding the first Spanish town in Peru, San Miguel de Piura. In September 1532 they began the climb up into the Andes towards the highland city of Cajamarca, where Atahualpa was resting his army at the hot springs.

The Battle of Cajamarca, 16 November 1532

The Battle of Cajamarca on 16 November 1532 may be the most disproportionate military encounter in recorded history. Atahualpa, surrounded by thousands of unarmed retainers in ceremonial dress, came out to meet Pizarro in the central plaza of the town. Friar Valverde read out the Requerimiento — the formal Spanish demand that the emperor accept the Catholic faith and Spanish authority — through the interpreter Felipillo. When Atahualpa picked up the Bible Valverde handed him, did not understand what to do with it, and dropped it, Pizarro’s men gave the prepared signal. Hidden cavalry, foot soldiers with steel swords, and small cannon attacked the unarmed retinue. Thousands of Inca died in the plaza. Atahualpa was seized.

Atahualpa offered an enormous ransom: a room about 22 feet by 17 feet filled once with gold and twice with silver. Indigenous porters carried the metal in for months. The treasure was eventually melted down and distributed among the Spaniards (worth tens of millions of pounds in modern terms). Pizarro had Atahualpa garrotted in the plaza of Cajamarca on 26 July 1533 anyway — condemned on charges of plotting against the Spanish, idolatry and the murder of Huascar. The execution had no clear justification under Spanish law and Charles V later expressed displeasure.

No — Pizarro arrived at the moment a civil war and an undocumented epidemic had already shattered Inca leadership. The historian Matthew Restall’s ‘Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest’ argues that the conquest of Peru, like the conquest of Mexico, was a coalition victory over a divided empire, not a Spanish solo achievement. Smallpox killed Huayna Capac. The civil war split the Inca army in two. Atahualpa’s execution removed the empire’s only recognised authority. Indigenous peoples Atahualpa had crushed in the civil war — the Cañari, the Huanca and Huascar’s old loyalists — allied with the Spanish. Top-band judgements weigh disease, civil war, surprise at Cajamarca, Spanish horses and steel, and Indigenous allies against each other rather than collapsing the conquest into one cause.

Cuzco and Lima

After Atahualpa’s execution, the Spaniards marched on Cuzco, the imperial capital, and entered the city in November 1533. They installed Manco Inca — another son of Huayna Capac — as a puppet emperor and looted the temple of Coricancha, melting down gold panels that had once lined its walls. In January 1535 Pizarro founded a new Spanish capital, Lima, on the Pacific coast — chosen so that Spanish ships could resupply quickly without climbing the Andes. The Inca empire’s political centre had shifted from a highland Indigenous city to a coastal Spanish one.

The Inca Revolt and Siege of Cuzco, 1536–37

The puppet, however, did not stay quiet. In 1536 Manco Inca slipped out of Cuzco and raised an army of perhaps 100,000 Indigenous warriors. From May 1536 to early 1537 he besieged Cuzco, which was held by a Spanish garrison under Hernando and Juan Pizarro. The siege of Cuzco was the closest the Inca came to driving the Spanish out: the city burned, Juan Pizarro was killed, and the small Spanish force was reduced to fighting from inside the cathedral and the fortified hills above the city. The siege was finally broken when reinforcements arrived from Almagro returning out of Chile and from Manco Inca’s Indigenous enemies switched sides. Manco himself retreated into the eastern jungle and founded a rump Vilcabamba state that lasted until 1572.

Key Fact

Manco Inca, installed by Pizarro as a puppet in 1533, raised an army of about 100,000 warriors and besieged Cuzco for ten months in 1536–37. He retreated to Vilcabamba, where the Neo-Inca state survived until 1572.

Impact

The conquest of Peru gave Spain a second continental empire to match New Spain. The Andean economy was reorganised around silver mining (Potosi was discovered in 1545, three years after the New Laws). Encomiendas were granted to conquistadors. The Quechua-speaking world entered a long, painful adjustment to Spanish rule. But the conquest also planted the seed of its own crisis: Pizarro and Almagro had been partners but were now rivals, and the conquistadors’ thirst for encomiendas would soon collide with Madrid’s attempt to centralise authority. The 1546 conquistador rebellion against the New Laws — led by Pizarro’s younger brother Gonzalo — was already in formation.

The two great conquests are remarkably similar. Both pivoted on a small Spanish force exploiting an empire weakened from inside — for Cortes the Tlaxcalan resentment and the Toxcatl rebellion; for Pizarro the Inca civil war and the death of Huayna Capac. Both depended on smallpox arriving ahead of or alongside the Spaniards (Tenochtitlan in 1520, the Andes around 1527). Both used the capture of a capital and a puppet emperor as the political endgame — Cuauhtemoc and Manco Inca played the same role. Both ended with conquistador civil wars over the spoils — Velazquez vs Cortes, Almagro vs Pizarro. Top-band judgement answers can use the comparison itself: the conquest of empires of millions by forces of hundreds is not explained by Spanish military superiority alone, but by a recurring pattern of Indigenous division, disease and coalition warfare.

Top-band answers chain events with phrases like ‘this in turn forced’ and ‘because of this’ — for example, smallpox killed Huayna Capac, which split the empire, which let Atahualpa fight a civil war, which left him exposed at Cajamarca. For Explain the Importance questions, weigh several factors against each other (the death of Huayna Capac, the civil war, surprise at Cajamarca, Spanish horses and steel, Indigenous allies) rather than collapsing the win into Spanish military genius. Use precise vocabulary — Quechua, Cajamarca, Vilcabamba, Requerimiento, encomienda — for SPaG marks, and write ‘Indigenous peoples’ rather than older terms.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Smallpox arrived in the Andes ahead of the Spaniards and killed Huayna Capac around 1527, triggering an Inca civil war between Huascar in Cuzco and Atahualpa in Quito. Atahualpa won the war just weeks before Pizarro arrived in 1532.
  • At the Battle of Cajamarca on 16 November 1532, Pizarro’s 168 men ambushed Atahualpa’s unarmed retinue, killed thousands and seized the emperor. Despite paying an enormous gold and silver ransom, Atahualpa was garrotted on 26 July 1533.
  • The Spanish entered Cuzco in November 1533 and Pizarro founded Lima in 1535. Manco Inca’s 1536–37 siege of Cuzco came close to reversing the conquest before Indigenous and Spanish reinforcements broke it; the rump Neo-Inca state survived at Vilcabamba until 1572.

practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant consequence; a further mark for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• The Inca empire was left without a recognised emperor — Huayna Capac’s named heir died at the same time, probably also of smallpox — opening the way for rival sons to claim the throne.
• A civil war broke out between Huascar in Cuzco and Atahualpa in Quito (1529–32), splitting the empire’s armies and elite into two warring camps.
• The civil war ended just weeks before Pizarro’s force reached Cajamarca, leaving Atahualpa’s veteran army exhausted and his political authority untested.
• Smallpox — almost certainly the cause of Huayna Capac’s death — reached the Andes ahead of the Spaniards via Indigenous trade routes, suggesting that European disease was already a force in Andean politics before any Spaniard arrived.

practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order in which they happened.

Indicative content:
• In 1528 Pizarro made a brief reconnaissance of the Inca coast at Tumbes, saw the wealth of the empire, and travelled to Spain to secure royal authority for a full conquest expedition (the Capitulation of Toledo, 1529).
• Meanwhile, smallpox — spreading south from Mexico through Indigenous trade routes ahead of the Spaniards — killed Huayna Capac and his named heir around 1527. This in turn left the throne disputed between Huascar in Cuzco and Atahualpa in Quito.
• Because of the disputed succession, the Inca empire fought a civil war from 1529 to 1532. Atahualpa’s veteran northern army defeated Huascar at the Battle of Quipaipan in spring 1532 — just weeks before Pizarro’s force began climbing into the Andes.
• This in turn meant that when Pizarro’s 168 men reached Cajamarca in November 1532, Atahualpa was a victor without a recognised state behind him — surrounded by an exhausted army of supporters but without the legitimacy of the emperor he had killed.
• Because of all this, Atahualpa accepted Pizarro’s invitation to meet in Cajamarca’s plaza unarmed. The ambush of 16 November 1532 killed thousands and seized the emperor — ending an empire of millions in a single afternoon.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with explicit linkage (‘this in turn forced’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (Capitulation of Toledo, Quipaipan, Cajamarca).
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Inca civil war (1529–32) for the Spanish conquest of Peru.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the civil war, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The civil war split the Inca army into two warring camps and consumed the empire’s most experienced commanders just before the Spaniards arrived — weakening the state militarily at the worst possible moment.
• Atahualpa won the war only weeks before Pizarro reached Cajamarca; his authority was therefore untested, and many of Huascar’s old loyalists later allied with the Spanish against him.
• The civil war made Indigenous allies available — the Cañari, the Huanca and Huascar’s supporters joined the Spanish coalition against Atahualpa, mirroring the Tlaxcalan alliance against the Aztecs.
• The civil war meant the Inca elite were politically divided. Pizarro could exploit those divisions by installing Manco Inca, another son of Huayna Capac, as a puppet emperor in 1533.
• Without the civil war, the conquest of Peru — like Cortes’s conquest of Mexico — could not have been a coalition victory over a divided empire. The historiographical move (Restall) is that conquest required Indigenous division, not Spanish genius.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (Cañari and Huanca allies, Manco Inca, Quipaipan, link to Restall’s framing).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the civil war without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the siege of Cuzco (1536–37) for Spanish rule in Peru.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the siege, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The siege was the closest the Inca came to reversing the conquest. Manco Inca raised an army of perhaps 100,000 Indigenous warriors and trapped a small Spanish garrison in the city for ten months.
• It showed that the conquest of 1532–33 had been incomplete. The puppet emperor system was unstable; Manco Inca slipped his Spanish handlers and turned the Inca state machinery against them.
• The siege killed Juan Pizarro, exposed the small size of the Spanish force, and forced Madrid to accept that holding Peru would require a permanent military presence and a properly governed colony — not just conquistadors and puppets.
• The siege was broken because Indigenous peoples Atahualpa had crushed during the civil war switched to the Spanish side, and Almagro’s force returned from Chile in time to relieve the city. Spanish rule in Peru depended on Indigenous allies in 1537 just as it had in 1532.
• Manco Inca’s retreat to Vilcabamba founded a rump Neo-Inca state that survived until 1572 — a long-term reminder that resistance was not finished, and a recurring problem for the colonial regime.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (Manco Inca, the size of his army, Juan Pizarro’s death, Almagro’s relief, Vilcabamba 1572).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the siege without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Atahualpa’s execution (26 July 1533) for the Spanish conquest of Peru.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Atahualpa’s execution, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The execution removed the only emperor with active authority over the Inca army — Huascar had already been killed earlier in the civil war — leaving the empire without a recognised central leader.
• It opened the way for the Spanish puppet emperor system. Manco Inca was installed in late 1533 with no legitimate alternative claimant alive.
• It allowed Pizarro to march on Cuzco unopposed by an organised state army; the city fell in November 1533 with relatively little resistance from the imperial centre.
• It set a brutal precedent for Spanish dealings with Indigenous rulers — even cooperation and ransom did not save Atahualpa — which would later make Indigenous leaders reluctant to negotiate.
• It created a long-term moral problem for Madrid. Charles V expressed displeasure at the execution; the legality and justice of the conquest became one of the key questions debated by Las Casas, Sepulveda and the New Laws.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (Huascar, Manco Inca, Cuzco 1533, Charles V’s reaction, link to Las Casas debate).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the execution without explaining its importance.

lessons.title: Viceroys, Encomiendas, Las Casas and the New Laws
lessons.description: Viceroys, encomiendas, and Las Casas’s challenge in the New Laws of 1542.
lessons.content_html:
A Government for Two Continents

By the early 1530s Spain controlled an empire so large that no governor could oversee it from Madrid. The crown had to invent a new layer of authority. The instrument was the viceroy — literally ‘in place of the king’. A viceroy held all royal power in a named territory: he commanded the army, presided over the courts, taxed, granted land and signed treaties with Indigenous peoples. In 1535, Charles V created the Viceroyalty of New Spain, with its capital at Mexico City. The first viceroy was Antonio de Mendoza, a careful administrator who served for fifteen years and centralised royal authority over the freelance conquistadors of Cortes’s generation. The Viceroyalty of Peru followed in 1542, with its capital at Lima. Underneath each viceroy sat an audiencia — a royal court of judges who heard appeals and supervised local governors.

Key Fact

The Viceroyalty of New Spain was established in 1535 with its capital at Mexico City and its first viceroy Antonio de Mendoza. The Viceroyalty of Peru was established in 1542 with its capital at Lima.

The Encomienda by 1540

Underneath the new viceroys sat an older system. The encomienda had begun on Hispaniola in the early 1500s and travelled with the conquistadors to Mexico in the 1520s and Peru in the 1530s. Tens of thousands of Indigenous people were now ‘entrusted’ to Spanish encomenderos. In law, the deal was that an encomendero collected tribute and labour from a named community in exchange for protecting them and instructing them in the Catholic faith. In practice, the encomienda was unpaid forced labour with a religious gloss. Encomenderos became a colonial aristocracy, enriching their families on land and labour they had not paid for.

Population collapse made the system worse, not better. As Indigenous communities shrank from disease, the same tribute demand fell on fewer people, intensifying the burden on the survivors. By the 1540s, in some areas, encomienda demands amounted to a death sentence for the workers under it.

Bartolome de las Casas

Bartolome de las Casas was the most important Spanish dissenter of the period. He was not an outsider but an insider — a former encomendero who had taken part in the conquest of Cuba (1511–15) and held an encomienda himself before his conversion of conscience. In 1514, after preparing a sermon on a passage in Ecclesiasticus, he renounced his encomienda and freed the Indigenous workers tied to it. He spent the next fifty years lobbying the Spanish crown to dismantle the system that he had once profited from.

Las Casas was not the first Spaniard to protest. The Dominican friar Antonio de Montesinos had preached the famous 1511 sermon on Hispaniola — ‘Are these not men?’ — the first public Spanish protest against the treatment of Indigenous peoples. But Las Casas was the most persistent. He travelled repeatedly between the Caribbean, Mexico, Peru and Spain. He wrote a stream of memoranda to the king. He was made ‘Protector of the Indians’ in 1516, a court advocate for Indigenous causes. In 1542 he gathered his arguments into a long memorandum for Charles V called the Brevisima relacion — the Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies — describing in detail the cruelty of the encomienda and conquest.

No — the period is full of internal Spanish conflict. Velazquez against Cortes; Pizarro against Almagro; Las Casas against Sepulveda; the crown against the encomenderos. Top-band judgement answers note this. The view that ‘everyone thought like that back then’ is historically false: the first sustained European argument for Indigenous human rights was made by a Spaniard. Showing Spain wrestling with itself — Montesinos in 1511, Las Casas’s renunciation in 1514, the New Laws debate in 1542, the Valladolid debate in 1550–51 — is a more historically accurate framing than ‘Spain conquered, the Church blessed it, and that was that’.

The New Laws, 20 November 1542

In November 1542 Charles V signed the New Laws. The document was a direct response to Las Casas’s lobbying. The most important provisions were these. First, the outright enslavement of Indigenous peoples was banned: the chains came off thousands of Indigenous workers across the Americas. Second, no new encomiendas would be granted. Third, existing encomiendas would expire on the holder’s death and revert to the crown — ending the colonial aristocracy within a generation. Fourth, royal officials, judges and clergy were forbidden from holding encomiendas. The principle behind the laws was radical: that Indigenous peoples were free vassals of the crown with rights, not the property of the conquistadors who had subdued them.

The 1546 Rebellion in Peru

The encomenderos in the Americas reacted with fury. The most violent reaction came in Peru. Blasco Nunez Vela arrived as the first viceroy in 1544 to enforce the laws. The encomenderos refused. They rose under Gonzalo Pizarro, the brother of the dead Francisco. In January 1546 Gonzalo’s men killed Nunez Vela at the Battle of Añaquito, and Gonzalo briefly ruled Peru as a rebel. Charles V was forced to compromise. He sent Pedro de la Gasca, a clergyman with full royal authority, who broke the rebellion and executed Gonzalo Pizarro in 1548 — but only after Madrid had quietly abandoned the inheritance clause. New encomiendas would still not be granted, but existing ones could now be inherited. The encomienda survived in weakened form for another two and a half centuries.

Key Fact

The New Laws of 1542 banned outright enslavement of Indigenous peoples, banned new encomiendas, and required existing ones to expire on the holder’s death. The 1546 conquistador rebellion in Peru, which killed Viceroy Nunez Vela, forced Madrid to repeal the inheritance clause — and encomiendas survived in weakened form.

Significance

Were the New Laws a success or a failure? The cleanest answer is: both. As a moral and legal landmark, they were enormous. The Spanish empire was the first European empire to formally debate the rights of conquered peoples and to write into law that Indigenous peoples had legal personality. The Valladolid debate of 1550–51 between Las Casas and the theologian Juan Gines de Sepulveda — over whether Indigenous peoples were ‘natural slaves’ in Aristotelian theory — was a debate Las Casas effectively won in moral terms. As an attempt to change the daily reality of colonial labour, the laws fell short. Encomiendas continued. The mita — the Indigenous forced-labour rota in the Andean silver mines — expanded after 1573. Top-band ‘importance’ answers weigh the laws as both a real reform and a partial failure, rather than picking one side. Las Casas died in 1566 still campaigning. His Brief Account, published in 1552, was reprinted across Protestant Europe and became the basis for the ‘Black Legend’ of Spanish cruelty — a propaganda weapon that hurt Spanish reputation but also kept the moral question alive.

In 1550 Charles V did something no European monarch had done before: he ordered all conquests in the Americas to pause until the morality of the conquest itself could be debated by a panel of theologians and lawyers in the Castilian town of Valladolid. Las Casas argued that Indigenous peoples were rational, fully human beings entitled to the same protection of natural law as Spaniards. Juan Gines de Sepulveda, drawing on Aristotle, argued that some peoples were ‘natural slaves’ whose conquest by a more advanced civilisation was morally justified. The panel never issued a clean verdict, but Las Casas’s arguments were broadly accepted as having defeated Sepulveda’s. The Valladolid debate did not stop the encomienda or the silver economy — but it established a principle that would echo for centuries: that conquered peoples have rights even against the state that has conquered them.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark Explain the Importance questions on the New Laws, the trap is treating them as a simple success or simple failure. Top-band answers weigh both: a genuine moral and legal landmark (banning enslavement of Indigenous peoples, establishing legal personality, opening the Valladolid debate) AND a partial reform (the inheritance clause was rolled back after the 1546 Peru rebellion, encomiendas survived for centuries). For 4-mark Consequence questions, focus on a specific dated outcome — for example, the 1546 rebellion that killed Viceroy Nunez Vela. Use precise vocabulary — viceroy, audiencia, encomienda, encomendero, Black Legend, Valladolid — for SPaG marks, and write ‘Indigenous peoples’ rather than older terms.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • By 1542, Spain governed its empire through two viceroyalties — New Spain (1535, capital Mexico City) and Peru (1542, capital Lima) — each backed by an audiencia of royal judges. The encomienda continued underneath, putting tens of thousands of Indigenous workers under Spanish encomenderos.
  • Bartolome de las Casas, a former encomendero turned Dominican friar, spent fifty years lobbying for Indigenous rights. His pressure secured the New Laws of 20 November 1542, which banned outright enslavement of Indigenous peoples and barred new encomiendas.
  • The 1546 conquistador rebellion in Peru — led by Gonzalo Pizarro, who killed Viceroy Nunez Vela — forced Madrid to repeal the inheritance clause. Encomiendas survived in weakened form for centuries; but the principle that Indigenous peoples had rights had been written into Spanish law.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the New Laws of 1542.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant consequence; a further mark for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• The outright enslavement of Indigenous peoples was banned, and many Indigenous workers held as slaves were freed across the Spanish Americas in the years that followed.
• The encomenderos — especially in Peru — rebelled. In January 1546 Gonzalo Pizarro’s men killed the first Viceroy of Peru, Blasco Nunez Vela, at the Battle of Añaquito.
• Charles V was forced to compromise: although the rebellion was eventually broken and Gonzalo Pizarro executed in 1548, the inheritance clause was quietly repealed. Existing encomiendas could now be inherited.
• The New Laws established the principle that Indigenous peoples had legal personality and rights as vassals of the crown, opening the way for the 1550–51 Valladolid debate between Las Casas and Sepulveda.

• The first Viceroy of New Spain, Antonio de Mendoza, used his fifteen-year tenure (1535–50) to centralise royal authority over the conquistadors, the encomienda and the audiencia.
• Each viceroyalty was supported by an audiencia — a royal court of judges — that supervised local governors and heard appeals, creating a layered bureaucracy quite unlike the personal rule of Cortes or Pizarro.
• The first Viceroy of Peru, Blasco Nunez Vela, was killed by encomenderos at the Battle of Añaquito in 1546 — showing that the viceroy system was not yet fully accepted on the ground.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Bartolome de las Casas in the period c1514–1552.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Las Casas, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Las Casas was the most persistent Spanish critic of the encomienda. As a former encomendero who renounced his grant in 1514, he had inside knowledge of the system — making his testimony harder to dismiss.
• He was made ‘Protector of the Indians’ at the Spanish court in 1516 and used the position for fifty years of lobbying, travelling repeatedly between the Americas and Spain.
• His memoranda to Charles V were the political pressure that produced the New Laws of 1542 — the first European law banning the outright enslavement of an Indigenous population.
• His Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (written 1542, published 1552) was reprinted across Protestant Europe and became the basis for the ‘Black Legend’ of Spanish cruelty — weaponised against Spain, but also a real moral indictment.
• He confronted the theologian Juan Gines de Sepulveda at the Valladolid debate of 1550–51, defending the position that Indigenous peoples were not ‘natural slaves’. The debate established the principle that Indigenous peoples had rights, even if the encomienda survived in practice.
• The historiographical move (Restall) is to see Las Casas as evidence that the conquest was contested by Spaniards in real time — not unanimously celebrated.

Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
