practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the encomienda system in the Spanish Empire by 1542.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the encomienda, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The encomienda was the everyday economic basis of the empire. Tens of thousands of Indigenous people in Mexico and Peru paid tribute and laboured under Spanish encomenderos — supplying food, cloth, building work and (later) labour for the mines.
• It created a colonial aristocracy. Conquistadors who had served in 1521 or 1532 were rewarded with encomiendas in lieu of cash, becoming wealthy landowners with hereditary expectations.
• It tied the missions to the labour system. Encomenderos were nominally responsible for the religious instruction of their workers, which gave the Franciscans and Dominicans access to Indigenous communities — including Las Casas himself.
• It became the central political problem of the empire. Las Casas’s campaign and the New Laws of 1542 were direct responses to encomienda abuses; the 1546 Peru rebellion was a direct defence of encomendero privilege.
• It demonstrated continuity rather than novelty. The encomienda often inherited Aztec and Inca tribute structures wholesale — the same workers paid the same tribute, but to a Spaniard rather than to Tenochtitlan or Cuzco.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (the link to missions, the link forward to the New Laws and the 1546 rebellion, the inheritance from Aztec and Inca tribute).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the encomienda without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the role of the viceroy in the Spanish Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of the viceroy, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The viceroy was the personal representative of the king in the colony, holding executive, judicial and military authority — allowing Madrid to govern at a distance of 9,000 kilometres.
• The first Viceroy of New Spain, Antonio de Mendoza, used his fifteen-year tenure (1535–50) to centralise royal authority over the conquistadors and the encomienda system, ending the era of personal conquistador rule.
• The viceroyalty system replaced the audiencia of 1528 with a single royal authority on the ground, supported by a permanent audiencia of judges underneath.
• The system spread the empire’s administration: Viceroyalty of New Spain (1535) for North and Central America, Viceroyalty of Peru (1542) for South America. Eighteenth-century New Granada and Rio de la Plata followed the same template.
• The system also exposed the limits of royal power. The first Viceroy of Peru, Blasco Nunez Vela, was killed by encomenderos in 1546 — showing that even royal authority needed military backing on the ground.
• The viceroys connect the period to the silver economy of the second half of the century. Viceroy Toledo of Peru (1569–81) would extend the mita forced-labour rota to feed the Potosi mines.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (Mendoza, Nunez Vela, the audiencia layer, link forward to Toledo).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the viceroy without explaining the role’s importance.

lessons.title: Silver, the Slave Trade and the Government of Empire
lessons.description: Silver, the slave trade and the bureaucracy that made Spain Europe’s superpower.
lessons.content_html:
A Mountain of Silver

In 1545 an Indigenous prospector called Diego Huallpa, traditionally credited with the discovery, found a vein of silver running through the cone-shaped mountain known as Cerro Rico — ‘rich hill’ — in the high Andes, in what is now Bolivia. The town that grew at its base, Potosi, would become for a century the most productive silver deposit in the world. A second strike followed in 1546 at Zacatecas in northern Mexico. Together they transformed the Spanish empire from a land of conquistadors and encomiendas into the financial superpower of Europe. Potosi alone is estimated to have produced about 60% of the world’s silver in the second half of the 16th century. By 1611, with around 160,000 inhabitants, the town high in the Andes was as populous as London or Paris.

Key Fact

Silver was discovered at Potosi (modern Bolivia) in 1545 and at Zacatecas (Mexico) in 1546. Potosi alone produced roughly 60% of the world’s silver in the second half of the 16th century.

La Paz and the Silver Road

Potosi’s silver had to reach Spain. In 1548 the Spanish founded the city of La Paz as a stopover on the silver road from the high Andes down to the Pacific coast and onward by treasure fleet to Seville. The road from Potosi over the high passes to Lima and the port of Arica was lined with mule trains carrying silver bars and food in the other direction. The town of La Paz became one of the wealthiest of the new colonial cities, in spite of the altitude and thin air at over 3,500 metres. The infrastructure of the silver economy — mule routes, mountain passes, port towns — reorganised Andean geography around extraction.

The Mita and the Cost of Silver

Mining at altitude in the 16th century was lethal work. Indigenous workers under the encomienda dug, hauled and refined the ore using mercury (also mined locally at Huancavelica from 1564), which poisoned them slowly. From 1573, under a later viceroy, the labour system was formalised as the mita — one in seven adult Andean men served four months a year in the mines, on rotation. The mita inherited a pre-Columbian Inca rota of the same name; the Spanish kept the form but turned it to their own purposes. Mortality rates were appalling. The mita is the deepest scar of the silver economy on Andean society: not the silver itself, but the bodies broken and the communities hollowed out to extract it.

How Spain Spent the Silver

By the 1550s, treasure fleets called flotas sailed from Cartagena and Havana to Seville under armed escort. The Spanish crown took a 20% tax called the quinto real — the royal fifth — on every ounce mined. The quinto became the biggest single source of revenue in Charles V’s European empire. But almost as fast as the silver arrived in Seville, it left again. Charles V was simultaneously Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain. He was at war on multiple fronts — against France in Italy, against the Ottoman Turks in the Mediterranean, against Lutheran princes in Germany, against the Protestant Dutch from the 1560s. He owed enormous debts to a German banking dynasty, the Fuggers, who had financed his 1519 election as emperor. Spanish silver flowed to German bankers to service Habsburg war debt. The empire was a great-power machine, not a national prosperity machine.

Mostly, no — not in the way students assume. The crown was rich on paper and a narrow elite of conquistadors, encomenderos and merchants did very well. But silver flooding into Europe drove a century of inflation — the ‘price revolution’ described by the 16th-century Spanish economists called arbitristas and the modern historian J.H. Elliott. Spanish goods became expensive and uncompetitive. Spanish manufacturing hollowed out. The crown went bankrupt repeatedly under Philip II. Top-band judgement answers note this paradox: the empire was Europe’s first lesson in how extraction can hollow out the extractor. Spain became powerful and dependent at the same time.

The Atlantic Slave Trade

Indigenous labour was not the only labour the empire used. From 1518, under licences called asientos, Spanish authorities allowed private contractors to ship enslaved Africans to the Americas. The numbers in the period 1518–55 were small relative to the later transatlantic slave trade — perhaps tens of thousands of enslaved Africans — but the legal structure, the Atlantic shipping routes and the asiento contracts that would underwrite three centuries of the trade were now in place. Enslaved Africans worked in the silver mines alongside Indigenous workers, on the early Caribbean sugar plantations, and as urban servants. The Caribbean shift towards African labour had begun on Hispaniola in the 1510s as the Taino population collapsed. The slow industrialisation of the trade in this period laid the foundation for what came later. The reform movement that produced the New Laws of 1542 banned the enslavement of Indigenous peoples but did not extend the same protection to enslaved Africans — a moral inconsistency Las Casas himself, in his old age, came to regret.

Key Fact

From 1518, the Spanish crown licensed the shipping of enslaved Africans to the Americas under the asiento system. Numbers in this period were modest, but the legal framework that would underwrite three centuries of the transatlantic slave trade was now in place.

Silver was not the only American product reshaping Spain. Sugar from the Caribbean plantations and tobacco from the mainland reached Seville in growing quantities and changed European diets. Cochineal — a brilliant red dye produced from an insect cultivated by Indigenous farmers in Mexico — became one of Spain’s most valuable American exports after silver. Crops travelled the other way too: maize, the potato, the tomato, the chilli pepper and cocoa would slowly transform European agriculture and cuisine over the next century. The Atlantic was becoming a single economic system, with Spain and its Seville monopoly at the centre of it. The historian J.H. Elliott describes this as the moment Spain ‘Atlanticised’ — reorienting from Mediterranean trade towards a new ocean-crossing empire.

The Government of Empire

By 1555 the Spanish empire had a working architecture. At the top sat the king. Underneath him in Seville sat the Council of the Indies, founded in 1524 as the supreme governing body for the Americas. The Council issued laws, appointed viceroys and audiencia judges, heard appeals and supervised colonial finances. Alongside it sat the Casa de Contratacion — the House of Trade, founded in 1503 — which regulated all shipping, trade, taxation, navigation and migration between Spain and the Americas. Every ship and every passenger was supposed to pass through Seville. Every quinto of silver was supposed to be recorded there.

Below these Spanish institutions sat the colonial layer: viceroys (New Spain from 1535, Peru from 1542), audiencias under the viceroys, governors and corregidores under the audiencias, and finally encomenderos, missions and mita rotas on the ground. The system was the most centralised European colonial bureaucracy of its century. It was also slow, paper-heavy and corrupt — orders from Madrid took months to reach Lima, and viceroys often complained that they could not carry them out. But the architecture endured. Latin American government and law would still be running on Spanish institutional templates two and a half centuries later.

An Empire at the End of the Period

By Charles V’s abdication in 1556, the Spanish Empire stretched from Mexico City to La Paz, from Havana to Manila (claimed via Magellan’s 1519–22 voyage and reached by Spanish ships in the 1560s). It was held together by the silver fleet, the asiento, the Council of the Indies and the Casa de Contratacion. It was the first global empire in human history. It was also dependent on extraction it could not control: silver to pay its wars, Indigenous and African forced labour to mine the silver, German bankers to lend against future fleets. The economic foundations of the next century were already visible in 1555, and so were the cracks. The conquest of the ‘New World’ had made Spain the dominant power of 16th-century Europe and prepared the long structural decline that would define its 17th century.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark Explain the Importance questions on silver, weigh both wealth (Potosi’s 60% of world silver, the quinto real, the silver fleet) and cost (the mita death toll, the price revolution that hollowed out Spanish manufacturing, dependence on the Fugger banking family). Top-band ‘importance’ answers refuse to pick one side. For 4-mark Consequence questions, focus on dated outcomes — the foundation of La Paz in 1548, the spread of the asiento slave trade, the silver-driven inflation of the price revolution. Use precise vocabulary — quinto real, asiento, mita, Casa de Contratacion, Council of the Indies, treasure fleet, price revolution — for SPaG marks, and write ‘Indigenous peoples’ and ‘enslaved Africans’ rather than older terms.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Silver discovered at Potosi (1545) and Zacatecas (1546) and the foundation of La Paz (1548) made Spain the financial superpower of 16th-century Europe. Potosi alone produced roughly 60% of the world’s silver in the second half of the century, taxed at 20% by the crown’s quinto real.
  • Almost as fast as silver arrived in Seville it left again, paying Charles V’s wars and the loans of the Fugger banking family. The price revolution hollowed out Spanish manufacturing, while the mita rota and the asiento slave trade extracted the human cost from Indigenous Andeans and enslaved Africans.
  • By 1555 the Spanish Empire had a working architecture — Council of the Indies (1524), Casa de Contratacion (1503), Viceroyalty of New Spain (1535), Viceroyalty of Peru (1542), audiencias, encomiendas and missions — the most centralised European colonial bureaucracy of its century, and the foundation of three more centuries of Spanish rule.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the discovery of silver at Potosi (1545) and Zacatecas (1546).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 4. 1 mark for identifying a relevant consequence; a further mark for development.

Indicative content (any two):
• Spain became the financial superpower of 16th-century Europe. Potosi alone produced roughly 60% of the world’s silver in the second half of the century, with the crown taking a 20% royal fifth (quinto real).
• The foundation of La Paz in 1548 as a stopover on the silver road from Potosi to the Pacific coast reorganised Andean geography around extraction.
• Indigenous labour conditions worsened. The mita system — formalised from 1573 but rooted in this period’s encomienda labour — sent one in seven Andean men into the mines for four months a year with appalling mortality.
• Silver flooding into Europe drove a century of inflation — the price revolution — which actually hollowed out Spanish manufacturing rather than enriching ordinary Spaniards.
• The crown’s share of silver went largely to German bankers (the Fuggers) to service Charles V’s European war debts, deepening Spain’s long-term dependence on extraction.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed in their own paragraph with specific dated detail.
Secure: Two consequences identified with brief development.
Developing: One consequence developed, or two listed under one heading.
Emerging: General comment on silver without a specific consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the asiento system (from 1518) for the Spanish Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 4.

Indicative content (any two):
• It legally formalised the Atlantic shipping of enslaved Africans to the Americas, creating the contractual framework that would underwrite three centuries of the transatlantic slave trade.
• It supplied labour for the early Caribbean sugar plantations, the silver mines and urban Spanish households — partially replacing the collapsing Indigenous Caribbean population.
• It exposed a moral inconsistency in Spanish reform: the New Laws of 1542 banned the outright enslavement of Indigenous peoples but did not extend the same protection to enslaved Africans — an inconsistency Las Casas himself eventually came to regret.
• It bound Spain’s American economy into Atlantic networks of trade, finance and migration that would shape European colonial economies for the next two centuries.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of silver from the ‘New World’ for the Spanish Empire in the period 1545–c1555.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of silver, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• Silver from Potosi (1545) and Zacatecas (1546) made Spain the financial superpower of 16th-century Europe. Potosi alone produced about 60% of the world’s silver in the second half of the century.
• The crown’s 20% tax (the quinto real) on every ounce mined became the biggest single source of royal revenue, financing Charles V’s wars in Italy, Germany, the Mediterranean and the Netherlands.
• Silver flowed almost as fast as it arrived to the Fugger banking family of Augsburg, who had financed Charles V’s election as Holy Roman Emperor in 1519. Spain’s European wars were paid for by Andean miners.
• Silver flooding into Europe drove the price revolution — a century of inflation that actually weakened Spanish manufacturing because Spanish goods became uncompetitive abroad.
• The human cost was extracted from Indigenous Andeans through forced labour rotas (which would be formalised as the mita from 1573), and from enslaved Africans shipped in under the asiento system.
• The historiographical move (J.H. Elliott) is that silver made Spain powerful and dependent at the same time — the empire was a great-power machine, not a national prosperity machine.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (Potosi, the quinto, the Fuggers, the price revolution, the mita).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of silver mining without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Council of the Indies (1524) and the Casa de Contratacion (1503) for the government of the Spanish Empire.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of these two bodies, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• The Council of the Indies (founded 1524) was the supreme governing body for Spanish America. It issued laws, appointed viceroys and audiencia judges, supervised colonial finances and heard final appeals — centralising authority over a continent in Madrid.
• The Casa de Contratacion (founded 1503) was the House of Trade in Seville. It regulated all shipping, trade, taxation, navigation and migration between Spain and the Americas. Every ship, passenger and ounce of silver was supposed to be registered there.
• Together the two bodies created the most centralised European colonial bureaucracy of the 16th century — quite unlike the personal rule of Cortes or Pizarro that they replaced.
• They allowed Madrid to enforce key reforms at scale, including the New Laws of 1542 and the assignment of viceroys to New Spain (1535) and Peru (1542).
• They were also slow, paper-heavy and limited by distance — orders from Seville often took months to reach Lima — explaining why the 1546 Peru rebellion succeeded for several years before being broken.
• The architecture endured: Latin American government and law would still be running on Spanish institutional templates two and a half centuries later.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (foundation dates, link to viceroyalties, link to the New Laws, the limits of distance).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the bodies without explaining their importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of enslaved African labour for the Spanish Empire in the period c1518–c1555.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of enslaved African labour, supported by accurate detail.

Indicative content:
• From 1518 the asiento system licensed the shipping of enslaved Africans to the Americas, creating the legal framework that would underwrite three centuries of the transatlantic slave trade.
• Enslaved Africans worked in the silver mines, on the early Caribbean sugar plantations and as urban servants — supplying labour as Indigenous Caribbean populations collapsed under disease and forced labour.
• African labour partially replaced the Tainos in Hispaniola and Cuba; by mid-century the demographic shift in the Caribbean was already underway.
• The asiento bound Spain’s American economy into Atlantic networks of trade and finance that would shape European colonial economies for the next two centuries.
• It also exposed the moral limits of the New Laws (1542): the laws banned enslavement of Indigenous peoples but not of Africans — an inconsistency that Las Casas eventually came to regret in his old age.
• Numbers in the period 1518–55 were small compared to the later trade, but the legal structures, shipping routes and contractual templates that would later move millions of enslaved Africans were now in place.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands with specific period detail (asiento, the Caribbean shift, the moral limits of the New Laws, the link forward to later centuries).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two listed with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the slave trade without explaining its importance.

practice_questions.text: Write an analytical narrative explaining how the ‘New World’ transformed the Spanish economy in the years 1503–c1555. You may use the following in your answer: the foundation of the Casa de Contratacion (1503), the discovery of silver at Potosi (1545). You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for a sustained narrative that explains how events connected, not just the order in which they happened.

Indicative content:
• In 1503 the crown founded the Casa de Contratacion in Seville to regulate all shipping, trade, taxation and migration to the Americas. This created the institutional framework for transatlantic commerce that would later channel a flood of bullion.
• In 1518 the first asiento licences began the legalised shipping of enslaved Africans to the Caribbean, supplying plantation and household labour as the Taino population collapsed.
• In 1521 the conquest of Tenochtitlan and the encomiendas Cortes granted there created a tribute economy that fed Spanish settlers from Indigenous labour without paying for it.
• This in turn drew Spanish settlers and capital across the Atlantic in greater numbers, supporting the further conquests of Peru (1532–33) and the foundation of Lima (1535).
• Because of this expansion, the discovery of silver at Potosi in 1545 had a system ready to move and tax it: mule trains down to the Pacific coast, ships to Panama, treasure fleets across the Caribbean to Seville, the quinto real recorded by the Casa de Contratacion.
• This in turn flooded Europe with silver, fuelling Charles V’s wars, enriching the Fugger bankers, but driving the price revolution that hollowed out Spanish manufacturing — making the empire both more powerful and more dependent.

Mastering: Sustained narrative analysis with explicit linkage (‘this in turn forced’, ‘because of this’). Both stimulus points used and developed; own knowledge clearly added (asientos, Tenochtitlan, Lima, the Fuggers).
Secure: Clear narrative with some analytical linkage; both stimulus points used.
Developing: Narrative is mostly chronological description; limited linkage between events.
Emerging: List of events without analytical connection.
